title: Processes for Pre- and Post-slaughter of Pig Slaughter Stock in an Abattoir

lessons.title: Pre-slaughter work: receiving and lairage
lessons.html:
Your work experience

In this module you work in the lairage and in the post-slaughter areas of a pork abattoir under a mentor. You must show that you can do the pre-slaughter and post-slaughter processes of that abattoir correctly and safely. Your mentor signs your logbook when you are competent.

Receiving pigs

  1. Check the delivery documents: farmer's name, number of pigs, and any information the abattoir requires about the pigs' health and medicine treatments.
  2. Count the pigs as they come off the truck and compare with the documents.
  3. Look at every pig. Report dead, injured, lame, sick or very weak pigs to the supervisor and the meat inspector at once.
  4. Off-load quietly with the ramp. Do not hit or kick pigs.

Lairage

  • Put pigs into clean pens without overcrowding. Keep groups from different farms apart where the plant requires it.
  • Check that water is available in every pen.
  • Write the pen number, farmer and count on the lairage board or record.
  • Pigs rest in the lairage before slaughter. Your plant sets the rest time.
  • Pigs that the meat inspector sets aside at the ante-mortem inspection go to the isolation or suspect pen.

Moving pigs to the stunning area

  • Move small groups with a pig board.
  • Keep pigs calm: no shouting, no rushing.
  • Do not let pigs pile up in the race.

Records you may complete

Receiving sheet, lairage count, mortality record (dead on arrival), and pen cleaning record. Fill them in honestly and sign them.

lessons.title: Post-slaughter work: after the line
lessons.html:
What happens after dressing

Post-slaughter processes start after the carcass has been dressed and inspected. During your work experience you will help with these tasks:

  • Following inspection decisions: moving passed carcasses on, putting detained carcasses on the detain rail, and taking condemned material to the condemned area. Only move detained carcasses when told to.
  • Final trim and wash of the sides.
  • Weighing each carcass and checking the number, mass and owner on the kill sheet.
  • Classification and marking: helping trained staff, and making sure marks and labels are clear.
  • Chilling: moving carcasses into the chiller, spacing them, and closing doors.
  • Offal handling: keeping edible offal clean and cold, and inedible material separate.
  • Dispatch: loading cold carcasses into clean, refrigerated trucks.

Loading for dispatch

  1. Check that the truck is clean and cold before loading.
  2. Check the order: which carcasses, how many, which customer.
  3. Hang carcasses on the truck rails so they do not touch the floor.
  4. Wear clean clothing and keep hands clean while handling carcasses.
  5. Complete the dispatch note and get it signed.

Safety

  • Carcass sides are heavy. Use the rails and hooks; do not carry heavy sides alone.
  • Chiller floors can be slippery and cold. Wear warm clothing and non-slip boots.
  • Know how to open the chiller door from the inside.

lessons.title: Showing competence and keeping evidence
lessons.html:
What your mentor checks

ProcessYou show that you
ReceivingCount pigs, check documents and report problems
LairageHandle pigs humanely, provide water, keep records
Inspection decisionsMove passed, detained and condemned carcasses correctly
Weighing and recordsRecord correct numbers and masses
ChillingSpace carcasses and record temperatures
DispatchLoad hygienically and complete the dispatch note

Building your logbook

  • Write each day: the date, the process you worked on and what you did.
  • Attach copies of records you completed if your provider allows it, such as a lairage sheet or chiller log.
  • Ask your mentor to observe and sign each process.
  • Write down problems you saw and how they were solved, for example: 'One pig arrived lame. I told the supervisor, and the meat inspector moved it to the suspect pen.'

Problems you must report

  • Pigs that are dead, injured, sick or without water.
  • Pig numbers that do not match the documents.
  • A chiller that is warm or a door that does not close.
  • A dirty truck at dispatch.
  • Any injury to you or another worker.

Reporting is part of competence. A worker who notices a problem and tells the right person quickly is doing the job well.

Key points

  • Count pigs, check documents and report sick or injured pigs on arrival.
  • Handle pigs calmly and make sure they have water in the lairage.
  • Follow the meat inspector's decisions on every carcass.
  • Weigh, record, chill and dispatch carefully and hygienically.
  • Keep your logbook up to date and signed by your mentor.
